strengths: Simple, well-motivated architectural idea: adding local text-to-text attention inside cross-attention layers (CASA) is an intuitive fix for the known fine-grained performance gap of cross-attention VLMs, and the paper provides a convincing controlled experiment (Fig. 1, Table 6) isolating the gap between insertion and cross-attention fusion.

Unusually thorough experimental evidence for an architecture paper: three fusion variants (CASA∨, ⊕, →) evaluated both when training a VLM from a text-only LLM and when adapting a frozen pretrained VLM (Qwen2.5-VL), plus controlled comparisons to vanilla and gated cross-attention trained in identical settings, Q-Former compression baselines, resolution ablations, and a per-layer efficiency profiling (Table 11).

The ablations directly probe the core hypothesis: Table 8 (masking self-attention vs. random tokens at inference) and the attention visualizations in Appendix A support the implicit-gating explanation, rather than relying only on end-task numbers.

Practically meaningful efficiency case: image tokens bypass FFNs and the KV cache, and the streaming video-captioning application (Figures 5, 6, Tables 9) demonstrates constant-memory, low-latency inference where insertion-based models OOM — a real, quantified advantage rather than a claim on paper.

Good attribution of prior cross-attention designs (mPLUG-Owl3, StreamChat, Flamingo lineage) and reproduction of baselines where public results are unavailable; training details and compute are documented in the appendix, supporting reproducibility (inference code and models released).
weaknesses: The core mechanism is a small modification of existing cross-attention designs; similar text-token-inclusion-in-attention ideas exist in the literature, so the novelty is incremental. The paper's strength lies in diagnosis and evaluation rather than a fundamentally new algorithm.

A persistent ~5-7% performance gap to token insertion remains, concentrated exactly on the fine-grained tasks (InfoVQA, ChartQA, AI2D) that motivate the work; 'largely closes the gap' in the abstract slightly oversells the image results (Tables 2, 3).

Baseline fairness concerns: the insertion baseline is trained at reduced resolution (672² vs. 896²) and shorter sequences due to memory constraints, so part of the reported insertion advantage (or CASA's deficit) is confounded by unequal training budgets and resolutions; Appendix C.3 itself shows resolution strongly affects the fine-grained benchmarks at issue.

The implicit-gating explanation is plausible but not conclusively established: the Table 8 '- SELF' ablation removes an attention path entirely, so severe degradation may reflect loss of information flow rather than gating specifically; the evidence is inferential and the mechanism is not tested against explicit gating at matched capacity in the adapted-VLM setting.

Evaluation relies on an LLM-as-judge (GPT-4o) protocol for the streaming captioning comparison against LiveCC, with non-matching model sizes (3B vs 7B) and no statistical treatment; this is a relatively weak signal for a headline application.

The 'implicit gating' claim vs. explicit gated CA is not fully disentangled — e.g., gated CA plus FFN image updates (StreamChat-style) is only partially ablated, and the CASA∨ variant sacrifices global text attention, raising questions about where CASA is genuinely preferable vs. merely cheaper.
Project-page URLs are left blank in the manuscript, and training code (only inference code and models are promised) is not clearly committed, somewhat limiting full reproducibility.

strengths: The core idea is simple, well-motivated, and clearly articulated: adding local text-to-text attention to cross-attention layers (CASA) provides an implicit gating effect, and the paper identifies lack of text-to-text interaction as a plausible root cause of the known cross-attention vs. token-insertion gap. The diagnostic framing (Figure 1, Figure 8, Appendix C.1) linking the observed literature gap to a controllable design choice is a genuine contribution to understanding.

Experimental evidence is extensive and reasonably controlled: three CASA variants (CASA→, CASA⊕, CASA∨), training from a text-only LLM and adapting a frozen pretrained VLM (Qwen2.5-VL), identical-setting comparisons against vanilla and gated cross-attention (Table 6a), and inference-time masking ablations (Table 8) that isolate the self-attention component. CASA consistently outperforms cross-attention baselines, including the 4x larger mPLUG-Owl3-8B on fine-grained tasks.

The efficiency analysis is honest and detailed: Table 1, Table 11, and Appendix C.2 carefully separate memory/compute effects of not passing image tokens through FFNs, image tokens used only as keys/values, and blockwise attention. The streaming video captioning application (Table 9, Figures 5-6) demonstrates a practical regime where insertion-based models hit OOM/context limits while CASA does not, supporting the paper's positioning.

Reproducibility is supported by plans to release inference code and trained models, public training data, detailed training configurations (Appendix B, Table 10), and re-evaluation of compared models with lmms-eval where public results were unavailable.

Limitations are acknowledged in the text rather than hidden: the residual ~5-7 point gap to token insertion (concentrated on InfoVQA/AI2D), the modest gains and high cost of FFN-based image embedding updates (Table 5), and the FlashAttention-2 causality caveat (footnote 1) are all stated openly.
weaknesses: The architectural contribution is incremental. CASA layers amount to cross-attention where keys/values also include a local causal text window. While the paper argues this differs meaningfully from prior gated cross-attention designs (mPLUG-Owl3, StreamChat, EVLM), the mechanism is a relatively small modification of a well-known operator, and the conceptual novelty beyond prior interleaved/local-attention hybrids is limited. The paper does not deeply situate CASA against blockwise/local-attention attention literature more broadly.

The evidence for the 'implicit gating' hypothesis is suggestive but not fully conclusive. Table 8 masks attention to self, which would degrade almost any attention layer, and Appendix A's attention-statistics analysis shows self-attention dominance rather than directly demonstrating a gating mechanism. A more rigorous analysis (e.g., controlled comparisons of explicit gating strength matched to CASA's effective gating, or gradient/attribution studies) would strengthen the causal claim.

Some baseline comparisons are confounded. The insertion-based Helium1 baseline is trained with shorter sequences (1024 vs. 2048 text tokens) and lower image resolution (672² vs. 896²) for memory reasons, so Table 2's gap partially mixes architecture with data budget. Table 12 mitigates this at inference, but a compute-matched or resolution-matched insertion baseline at training time is not fully provided. Comparisons to StreamChat are also incomplete since its results/models are unavailable.

The remaining gap to insertion is non-trivial on exactly the fine-grained tasks the paper emphasizes (e.g., InfoVQA 59.6 vs. 71.6 when adapting Qwen2.5-VL; ~12 points), so the claim of 'closing the gap' should be read carefully — the gap is substantially narrowed but not closed, and the paper's abstract wording slightly overstates this.

The LiveCC captioning evaluation relies on an LLM-as-judge protocol with GPT-4o-generated reference captions, and the best CASA model (39.4% winrate at 17k steps) still trails LiveCC-7B; the streaming results are compelling on memory/latency but the quality comparison is weaker and judge-based evaluation is noisy.

The CASA∨ variant has a non-obvious behavior (best when replacing few, uniformly placed self-attention layers) that is documented but not well explained, leaving some design decisions empirical rather than principled.

strengths: The core insight is well-motivated and clearly articulated: the performance gap between cross-attention and token-insertion VLMs is largely attributable to the absence of text-to-text interaction during visual injection, and the proposed CASA mechanism (concatenating local text tokens as keys/values within cross-attention) is a simple, elegant fix that retains the efficiency advantages of cross-attention.

The experimental evidence is unusually thorough for an architecture paper: controlled training-matched comparisons against vanilla and gated cross-attention (Table 6), three CASA variants, adaptation of both a text-only LLM and a pretrained VLM (Tables 2-4), an inference-time masking ablation that directly supports the implicit-gating claim (Table 8), attention visualizations (Fig. 7), placement ablations for CASA-v (Table 7), and an efficiency analysis with profiler measurements (Tables 1, 11).

The streaming live video captioning application (Sec. 4.5) convincingly demonstrates a practical benefit that token insertion cannot offer (constant memory and latency), backed by memory/wall-time measurements and a competitive winrate against larger LiveCC models.

The paper is transparent about limitations: it explicitly acknowledges a remaining ~5-7% gap to token insertion, discusses the FlashAttention-2 causality footnote, and analyzes where the gap concentrates (InfoVQA, AI2D).
Reproducibility is supported by released inference code, trained models, full training details (Table 10, Appendix B), and use of the standard lmms-eval harness.
The idea is compatible with existing efficient attention implementations and is modular (can be inserted into or replace self-attention layers in existing LLMs), which increases its potential impact.
weaknesses: A meaningful gap to token insertion remains (~7 points average for CASA from scratch; ~5 points for the Qwen2.5-VL adaptation, with large drops on InfoVQA (-12) and AI2D (-5)), so CASA 'closes the gap' only partially; the framing in places (e.g., 'closes much of the gap') slightly overstates the result relative to Table 3.

Comparisons with insertion baselines are not perfectly matched: InsertionHe-2B was trained at lower resolution (672^2 vs 896^2) and shorter sequences due to memory constraints. While Table 12 partially addresses this at inference time, a fair comparison at equal training compute/memory budget would strengthen the claims; conversely, this asymmetry means CASA may partly benefit from a larger effective training configuration.
All experiments are limited to 2B-3B scale models; it is unclear whether the gains persist at 7B+ scale or with stronger backbones, and the streaming claim relies on a single 3B model.

The streaming captioning evaluation (Table 9) uses GPT-4o both for generating reference captions and as the judge, and comparisons to LiveCC baselines are taken from the original paper rather than re-run; winrates across training steps also plateau/regress (39.4 at 17k vs 39.0 at 20k) without error bars or variance analysis anywhere in the paper.

The mechanistic explanation for why self-attention within CASA layers helps (implicit gating) is supported mainly by correlation (masking ablation, attention statistics); no direct causal test against alternative explanations (e.g., gradient flow, representational capacity, or simply an extra residual pathway) is provided.

Some related-work comparisons are incomplete: StreamChat results are largely unavailable/not reproduced, and comparisons to other efficient-insertion or KV-cache-compression streaming approaches (StreamingVLM, Flash-VStream) are discussed qualitatively but not evaluated head-to-head.

Minor: the paper contains some typos (e.g., 'mPlug-Own3-8B', 'mPLUG-Owl' naming inconsistencies, 'not do they' in the conclusion) and the project-page URLs are blank in the manuscript, which affects verification of released artifacts at review time.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly framed analysis: the paper systematically decomposes the difference between cross-attention (CA) and token insertion into five design elements (D1–D5), which is a useful conceptual contribution for understanding fusion mechanisms in VLMs and explains why prior CA models underperform.

Controlled experimental design: comparisons are run in identical training settings (same data, pipeline, compute budget) both from a text-only LLM (Helium1-2B) and by adapting a pretrained Qwen2.5-VL-3B, which is the right methodology to isolate architectural effects and corrects what appears to be an unfair impression of CA in the literature.

Strong practical results: vanilla CA comes within ~1.5 points of matched token insertion on average, and the adapted Qwen-CA model outperforms prior CA-based VLMs of larger size (mPLUG-Owl3, StreamChat), demonstrating that the previously reported gap was largely an artifact of training pipelines.

Compelling efficiency analysis (Table 1) and a real-world application (live video captioning on LiveSports3K) that shows near-constant memory/latency for CA versus OOM/latency growth for insertion, including a fair comparison against token compression baselines (Q-Former) that compression alone does not solve the streaming bottleneck.

Extensive ablations: layer frequency, parameter sharing, CAt+v windows, image token FFN updates, token compression, image resolution sensitivity, and training curves; good reproducibility posture with inference code, trained models, and detailed appendix (data mixture, schedules, architecture details).
weaknesses: Scale of evidence is limited to 2B/3B models; it is not established that the CA–insertion gap (~1.5–7%) and the design-element analysis hold at larger scales (7B+), where representational capacity may interact differently with frozen image tokens (D4).

Residual performance gaps are acknowledged but not resolved: ChartQA, InfoVQA, and DocVQA show persistent deficits relative to insertion (the D2/D4 components help but the trade-off analysis remains at the level of observation rather than explanation), and the claimed cause of these gaps is left speculative.

Some comparisons against prior CA models (e.g., StreamChat, mPLUG-Owl3) partially conflate architecture with training pipeline: the improvement over larger prior CA models mainly demonstrates the importance of a modern recipe, so the architectural superiority claim should be stated more carefully.

The gist-token mechanism for multi-image/video history is heuristic (reusing Qwen's post-image delimiter) and its effectiveness is evaluated only indirectly (small average drops); no dedicated ablation quantifies how much history information gist tokens retain or how performance scales with video length.

Measurement rigor gaps: results are single-run with no variance or significance estimates; the FFN-update ablation uses a frozen image encoder for memory reasons, weakening the direct comparison to prior work that trains these components.

Minor writing/presentation issues: broken project-page URL in the abstract, several typos (e.g., 'accumulatio steps insteas', 'improves performance (≈2 percents)'), a likely miscitation (ref [44], a 3D medical imaging paper, cited for context compression/gist tokens), and inconsistent referencing between Table 4(a) and 'Figure 4(a)'; Table 8 also appears to have missing entries.
No societal-impact discussion, and the D5 setting (single-frame windows) means the model cannot re-attend to raw past frames, a limitation for long-video QA that deserves more prominent treatment.

strengths: The paper provides a genuinely useful and well-motivated empirical analysis: the decomposition of CA vs. token insertion into five design axes (D1-D5) is clear, insightful, and gives the community a vocabulary for reasoning about fusion mechanisms beyond the 'CA underperforms' folklore.

The controlled experimental design is a major strength: training CA and insertion-based models under identical data, resolution, and token budgets (64 H100s, matched token counts) directly addresses the confounds that plague prior comparisons between CA and insertion VLMs.

Two complementary settings (training from a text-only LLM, and adapting a strong pretrained insertion VLM) strengthen the claims, and the lightweight adaptation result (retaining most of Qwen2.5-VL performance with only CA layers + last 4 vision blocks trainable) is practically significant.

The streaming/live video captioning demonstration concretely substantiates the efficiency claims with measured memory, FPS, and wall-time results (Fig. 4, Tab. 1), rather than only theoretical complexity arguments.

Good ablation coverage: layer frequency, parameter sharing, image-token FFN updates, token compression, and evaluation-resolution sweeps, plus per-step training curves that aid reproducibility of the training-efficiency findings.
The paper is honest about where CA still falls short (chart/infographic understanding), which adds credibility rather than overselling.

The work is appropriately positioned as an analysis/empirical study rather than a novel algorithm; for that contribution type, the evidence is adequate and the significance for practitioners (e.g., streaming VLM design) is real.
weaknesses: The scientific novelty is limited: the mechanisms examined (parameter sharing, local windowed attention with text keys, layer replacement, gist tokens, FFN updates on visual tokens) are all drawn from prior work (Flamingo, mPLUG-Owl3, StreamChat, gist tokens); the contribution is a careful re-evaluation, which may disappoint readers expecting a new method or a deeper causal/theoretical account of why CA lags on InfographicVQA/ChartQA.

The persistent gap on chart/document/infographic understanding (e.g., 57.4 vs. 77.1 on InfoVQA in Tab. 3) is acknowledged but unexplained; the paper identifies where CA fails but does not diagnose why, which weakens the analytical contribution.

Scale is limited (2B/3B backbones); all conclusions about CA competitiveness are drawn at small scale, and it is unclear whether the gap to insertion grows with model/data size, especially given the remainder of the gap on fine-grained tasks.

Several presentation and citation issues: the project-page URL is missing in the abstract; reference [44] (VoCo, a 3D medical image contrastive-learning paper) appears miscited in the context-compression discussion; 'improves' should be 'improves'; these undermine polish and raise questions about overall care.

Only inference code and trained models are promised; training code and data mixture configuration would be needed for full reproducibility of the controlled comparison, which is the paper's core contribution.

The LiveCC comparison (Tab. 4a) compares a 3B CA model against reported numbers of a 7B baseline using an LLM-as-judge protocol; win-rate results near ~39% vs. 41-43% are treated as 'similar,' and no variance or multiple-judge robustness is reported.

Some efficiency comparisons (Tab. 1) conflate design choices; e.g., the CAt+v memory advantage relative to insertion depends on window/gist-token count choices that are not fully ablated, so the efficiency claims should be read as setting-dependent rather than general.
Societal impact and limitations are not explicitly discussed (only implicit limitations), which for an analysis paper that will inform architecture choices would have been a valuable addition.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly framed research question: the paper asks whether the underperformance of cross-attention (CA) VLMs reflects fundamental architectural limits or merely differences in training pipelines, and provides a convincing controlled answer.

The decomposition of the CA-to-token-insertion gap into five design elements (D1-D5) is insightful and gives the community a useful conceptual framework; the intermediate variants (CA_phi, CA_{t+v}, CA_<) form a coherent design space with measured efficiency-performance trade-offs.

Careful controlled experimental design: CA and insertion models are trained under identical conditions (data, resolution, token budgets), which is exactly the comparison missing from prior literature. The from-scratch (Helium1-2B) and adaptation (Qwen2.5-VL-3B) settings complement each other nicely.

Strong empirical results: vanilla CA narrows the gap to ~1.5% average vs. matched token insertion, and the adapted Qwen2.5-VL CA model outperforms prior CA-based SotA (mPLUG-Owl3 7B) at smaller scale, notably on document/chart tasks.

The live video captioning application (Sec. 4.5) convincingly demonstrates the practical value of CA: near-constant memory and latency over long streams, with wall-time and OOM measurements contrasting against token insertion and Q-Former compression.
Good reproducibility posture: public data, released models and inference code, detailed appendix (training schedules, hyperparameters, resolution ablations).
Honest reporting of limitations: the persistent gaps on ChartQA/InfographicVQA are clearly acknowledged rather than hidden, and the D4 (FFN updates) trade-off is quantified rather than dismissed.
weaknesses: Limited novelty in a strict algorithmic sense: the components (vanilla CA, parameter sharing, windowed attention, gist tokens) are largely known; the contribution is primarily an empirical analysis and feasibility study. This is acceptable for the contribution type, but the paper does not fully articulate this framing.

The significant residual gap on InfographicVQA (~20 points for the adapted Qwen model) and ChartQA is substantial and only partially explained; the paper offers little analysis of why fine-grained document tasks specifically suffer under CA.

The gist-token mechanism, which is central to the video results, is somewhat ad hoc (reusing Qwen's post-image delimiter tokens as gist tokens) and is not thoroughly ablated: no study of the number of gist tokens, learned vs. delimiter tokens, or sensitivity to window length.
Experiments are restricted to 2B-3B scale; it remains unclear whether the observed near-parity holds at 7B+ scale where the paper draws its most consequential comparisons against the literature.

Some evaluations have methodological caveats: the LLM-as-judge live captioning comparison to LiveCC is not strictly apples-to-apples (different training trajectories/steps), and the FFN-update ablation freezes the image encoder, confounding the comparison somewhat.
No error bars or variance estimates for the reported gaps; several conclusions rest on 1-3 point differences across benchmarks where evaluation noise can be non-trivial.
Table 8 appears to have missing values for the CA model at 1400 resolution (InfoVQA column), suggesting some sloppiness in the results presentation.
Reproduction of the training experiments requires 64 H100 GPUs, which limits community verification, even though inference code and models are released.
